  caption: Based on the findings summarized in Table 3, several generalizable guidelines for optimizing the processing parameters of glass–ceramics can be synthesized. Analysis across machining techniques reveals consistent trends that form a coherent framework for practical application. First, the adjustment of core machining parameters — cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut — profoundly influences surface quality and integrity. For instance, in grinding and turning operations, combining higher cutting speeds with lower feed rates and shallower depths of cut generally leads to reduced Ra and minimized SSD, as evidenced in studies on materials such as Zerodur® (under grinding optimal process parameters, the MRR was as high as 1528.3 mm3/min, and the Ra was reduced to 10 nm [66]). This highlights the critical balance between achieving high MRR and preserving surface integrity. Second, the selection of tooling and abrasive conditions consistently contributes to enhanced outcomes. The use of finer abrasives in grinding, optimized tool geometries in turning, and tailored polishing tools in finishing processes all promote improved surface finish and reduced residual stresses. Furthermore, structured optimization methodologies — such as RSM and simulation-based approaches — have proven effective in systematically identifying optimal parameter sets, reinforcing the value of data-driven process design. In traditional polishing, controlled polishing time has been shown to improve gloss and translucency without compromising mechanical properties, indicating that time-dependent parameters also require careful calibration (60 s of manual polishing, the gloss reached 85.02 ± 12.94 GU [70]). Overall, these observations suggest that, regardless of the specific glass–ceramic material or machining technique, a universal optimization framework can be adopted. This framework emphasizes the careful balancing of speed, feed, and depth parameters; the strategic selection of tools and abrasives; and the application of systematic, model-assisted optimization methods. Collectively, these principles provide transferable and practical guidance for engineers and researchers seeking to optimize glass–ceramic machining processes across a wide range of applications.

  caption: The k of a gas is independent of pressure in the near atmospheric pressure range, and it becomes dependent on the magnitude of pressure at high or very low pressure [22]. At very high pressure (around 1 GPa), most gases transform into liquid or solid, causing a rapid increase in their k [23]. The k of liquids such as water, toluene, silicon oil, and methanol-ethanol increases with pressure, and it grows rapidly at higher pressure due to the solidification process [23]. In the case of pebble beds, the k depends on various parameters, such as $k _ { p } , k _ { g } ,$ the ratio of pebble to gas conductivity $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$ , gas pressure, bed packing fraction, pebble size, pebble surface roughness, contact area and bed deformation [24]. Pebble beds of lithium ceramics are selected for the tritium breeding material for the solid breeder concept of fusion reactors. Properties of these pebble beds in different thermo-mechanical conditions are necessary to design the breeder units of fusion reactors. Following are the experimental studies investigating the effects of compressive stress, temperature, and filling gas (gas in the voids between pebbles) pressure on the k of pebble beds. An earlier study has measured the k of LOS and different types of LMT pebble beds for deformation up to 4.5 % and temperature up to 800 ◦C using hot-wire method [25]. The study reported about a 20 % increase in k at a maximum temperature in the air environment, and this effect was reported to increase with decreasing temperature. Another study was carried out to measure the k of a binary-sized LMT pebble bed and found it increasing with an increase in strain of the pebble bed [26]. At temperatures ranging from 400 ◦C to 700 ◦C, the k of the LMT pebble bed was found to increase with compressive deformation [27]. Beryllium pebble bed’s k was also reported to increase with compressive stress [28]. A recent study [29] investigated the k of LOS and other advanced ceramic breeder pebble beds and confirmed the rise in k with compressive stress using the transient probe method. LMT pebble bed’s k was also observed to increase with stress in the helium environment [30]. Another recent experiment [31] also confirmed the increasing trend of k in titanium beryllide pebble beds. A recent study [32] utilised the laser flash method to measure the k of LMT pebble bed under compressive stress and observed a similar trend. Compressive stressdependent anisotropic k of powdered titanium (particle size: 45–150 μm) and spherical copper shot (particle size: 595–841 μm) was measured using needle probes [33]. The study concluded that k is an anisotropic property for granular particle beds under uniaxial compression, and the vertical k increases at a higher rate than the horizontal k with increasing stress. Fig. 1 contains the literature data of k of LOS and LMT pebbles under compression. The bottom X-axis represents the percentage strain of the bed for strain-based measurements, and the top X-axis represents stress in MPa for stress-based measurements. The plot’s data points represent strain-based measurement unless mentioned otherwise in the legends section. It is to be noted that the strain-based measurement data points are not related to the stress value on the top X-axis and vice versa. As the plot shows, the k of the pebble beds increases with compressive stress in air and helium environments. It can be observed that an increase in k is more prominent in the air environment than helium because of the higher pebble-to-gas conductivity ratio $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$

  caption: Implant Materials For decades, biocompatible ceramics and glasses have been regarded as implant materials for repairing injured hard tissues (bone and teeth) [142,143]. However, widely utilized ceramic materials have struggled to meet the growing demand for higher strength and shorter bone healing periods [144], necessitating the development of high-strength bioactive glass-ceramics with controllable resorption periods. The core challenge is reconciling bioactivity (often linked to solubility) with long-term mechanical stability and biocompatibility. Glass-ceramics, with their excellent mechanical properties and osteoconductivity, can be applied for the repair and reinforcement of mineralized tissues [145–147], and they are widely applied in other fields such as bone transplantation, maxillofacial surgery, dentistry, and bone implantology [148]. In bone implant research, Baino et al. [149] Proposed an innovative all ceramic acetabular cup for hip prosthesis, as shown in Fig. 14a. da Rocha Barros et al. [150] implanted high-strength silicate glass-ceramic into rabbit femurs and found that it exhibited good biocompatibility but poor osteoinductivity, along with obvious dissolution problems in the biological environment (solubility of 1244 mg/cm2). This led to particle detachment from the material surface, inducing inflammation and fibrosis. These findings suggested that although glass-ceramics had potential for bone implantation, their chemical stability required further optimization. In addition, Savvova et al. [151] studied the potential of reinforced bioactive calcium phosphate-silicate glass-ceramics for dynamic loading applications in orthopedics. The results showed that glass-ceramics containing 60 vol% hydroxyapatite exhibited biocompatibility and mechanical properties (KIC = 2.8 MPa m1∕2, HV = 3800 MPa) close to those of bone tissue after short-term heat treatment, providing an important reference for the development of orthopedic implants. In the field of orbital implants, Francesco Baino and his team reported the feasibility of glass-ceramic porous orbital implants made from calcium silicate glass [152–154]. Baino et al. [155] prepared porous glass-ceramic artificial eye sockets using the sponge replication method. Studies showed that their Ra (Ra approximately 300 nm) was significantly lower than that of commercially available aluminum oxide implants (Ra approximately 750 nm). These implants exhibited excellent mechanical strength and biocompatibility, promoting post-surgical tissue fibrovascularization growth, and demonstrated their potential as lowcost, high-performance ophthalmic implant materials. Subsequently, Ayawanna et al. [156] employed eggshells as raw materials to prepare porous glass-ceramic orbital implants with a porosity of more than 30% (aesthetic eye prosthesis shown in Fig. 14a) and obtained a pure biocompatible $\mathrm { C a S i O } _ { 3 }$ phase at $1 1 0 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Such materials not only had good chemical stability but also supported the inward growth of fibrous vascular tissue while significantly reducing costs, providing a possible alternative to traditional expensive implant materials. The synthesis of these findings yields a fundamental guideline: effective bone implants require a tailored dissolution rate—sufficient to foster bioactivity and integration but controlled enough to maintain mechanical function over the intended service life. This is achieved by precise management of glass network modifiers, crystalline phase selection, and porosity.

  caption: A key mission for the next-step fusion tokamak device China Fusion Engineering Test Reactor (CFETR) is demonstrating tritium self-sufficiency, which requires a sufficiently high tritium burnup fraction $( f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } )$ in order to match a practically achievable tritium breeding ratio (TBR) with the blanket design constraints. Core-edge coupling simulations are performed to investigate the dependence of $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ on different controlling parameters for CFETR scenarios. Core plasma profiles with a range of pedestal densities are simulated by consistent iterative calculations of equilibrium, transport, auxiliary heating and current drives within the OMFIT framework. The core-SOL integrated COREDIV code is then used to evaluate $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ with the OMFIT modelled core plasma parameters as input. According to the simulations, fburnup can be effectively increased with a higher pedestal density on account of the fusion power increasing faster than the fueling source required to maintain steady-state. Higher $n _ { \mathrm { e , s e p } } / n _ { \mathrm { e , p e d } }$ can also increase the $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ due to increase of fuel recycling. Deeper pellet fueling deposition and lower ratio of particle to thermal diffusivities $D / \chi$ can both increase the effective particle confinement time and thus $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } .$ . However, the effect of helium and other impurities (Ar and W) is shown to reduce $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ for comparable impurity and main ion transport. Based on our analysis, using present pellet fueling technology, achieving $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } > 3 \%$ for CFETR will be very challenging. This is a lower limit for the required TBR $( > 1 )$ to match the achievable TBR for tritium self-sufficiency. Furthermore, our study suggests that if fueling can penetrate deeper than $r / a < 0 . 8$ under optimistic conditions, the required burnup fraction could be attainable. The modelling results thus provide important suggestions and implications for the optimization of CFETR scenarios and development of advanced fueling systems.

To address the research question regarding structural optimization, it is clear that no single synthesis route is universally superior.
Solid-state synthesis offers scalability, while sol-gel and combustion methods provide superior microstructural control.
The choice of route must be guided by the specific requirements for tritium release kinetics and mechanical resilience.
It is known that future work should focus on optimizing dopant concentrations and sintering profiles to simultaneously enhance porosity for tritium diffusion and density for mechanical strength.

This dual optimization is essential for achieving the high breeding ratios and long-term structural stability required in fusion reactor applications.

title: Research Limitations and Future Directions
final:
# Research Limitations and Future Directions

It is known that irradiation-induced changes to the chemical, physical, mechanical, and thermal properties of solid breeding ceramics are integral to the selection of materials for fusion reactor applications. While $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ and $\mathrm{Li}_4\mathrm{SiO}_4$ are widely recognized as promising candidates due to their robust performance before and after irradiation, significant discrepancies remain in the literature regarding irradiation swelling and thermal conductivity degradation. These variations are essential to understanding the true limits of material longevity, yet direct comparison across studies is hindered by inconsistencies in grain size, pellet density, irradiation conditions, and testing methods. Consequently, it is essential to establish standardized testing protocols for long-term tritium breeding performance validation to resolve these unresolved discrepancies.

To address these limitations, an Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) framework is proposed to accelerate ceramic formulation. By synthesizing experimental data with computational models, researchers can predict material behavior under extreme conditions, thereby reducing the reliance on extensive physical trial-and-error. This approach is essential to understanding if a given material can withstand the complex interplay of thermal and mechanical stresses inherent in fusion environments. Furthermore, advanced manufacturing techniques, such as additive manufacturing, offer a pathway for fabricating complex blanket geometries with tailored porosity. While specific parameters for lithium ceramics are still being defined, the ability to control microstructure at the nanoscale is critical for enhancing mechanical integrity and tritium release efficiency.

Finally, the development of composite breeder systems incorporating neutron multiplying materials, such as beryllium, necessitates more standardized and controlled experiments. The creation of a comprehensive, vetted materials database, alongside the application of emerging AI/ML tools, provides a promising pathway for streamlining the selection of fusion reactor components. It is known that leveraging these data-driven approaches will uncover hidden correlations in large datasets, ultimately accelerating the deployment of reliable fusion energy systems.

title: Conclusions and Material Selection Criteria
final:
**Conclusions and Material Selection Criteria**

The selection of solid breeder ceramics for next-generation fusion reactors requires a rigorous synthesis of tritium breeding efficiency, mechanical durability, and fabrication scalability. This section addresses the critical research questions regarding which ceramic materials demonstrate the most promise and the current state of knowledge concerning irradiation effects on breeding ceramics.

**Comparative Performance and Material Selection**
The comparative performance of lithium titanate ($\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$) and lithium zirconate ($\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$) remains a central decision point in breeder blanket design. While both materials are viable candidates, their selection depends on balancing tritium release kinetics against thermal stability. $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ is often favored for its superior tritium release properties at lower temperatures, making it suitable for specific thermal regimes. Conversely, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$ is frequently preferred for its chemical stability, though it may require higher operating temperatures to achieve efficient tritium release. The definitive recommendation for next-generation deployment is not a singular material choice, but rather a holistic assessment that prioritizes materials demonstrating a favorable balance between high tritium recovery rates and the mechanical robustness necessary to withstand reactor environments. Solid breeders remain the top choice for primary blanket options due to their ease of fabrication, scalability, and reliable tritium recovery [17, 18], whereas liquid breeders are generally secondary candidates due to safety and production concerns [12].

**Irradiation Effects and Knowledge State**
Understanding irradiation effects on solid breeder material candidates is pivotal towards their implementation within fusion reactors. A major aspect of breeder selection revolves around how neutron irradiation affects the mechanical and thermal properties of Li-ceramic compositions. The current state of knowledge indicates that while pre-irradiation properties are well-documented, there is a critical gap in comprehensive post-irradiation data. Determining how irradiation may impact material properties is a vast region of research actively being explored by measuring pre-irradiation and post-irradiation values. Specifically, understanding if a given material can withstand long-term neutron exposure without significant degradation in thermal conductivity or mechanical strength is essential to validating its viability. While neutron irradiation is of most concern, other irradiation paths are also discussed for a comprehensive review, as alternative techniques are often used to simulate neutron irradiation degradations.

**Path to Engineering-Scale Deployment**
To transition from laboratory-scale breeder materials to engineering-scale deployment, future research must prioritize the validation of these irradiation effects under realistic reactor conditions. This includes establishing standardized protocols for measuring post-irradiation thermal conductivity and crush strength, which are currently insufficiently documented for long-term performance prediction. The scalability of fabrication methods is equally critical; for instance, the extrusion method used for $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ pebbles offers a pathway to engineering-scale production, whereas other synthesis methods require precise control over stoichiometry to maintain mechanical resilience. Ultimately, the successful demonstration of scalable fabrication techniques that maintain desired microstructural and thermal properties after extended neutron exposure will determine the definitive selection of breeder materials for future fusion reactors.

  caption: Based on the findings summarized in Table 3, several generalizable guidelines for optimizing the processing parameters of glass–ceramics can be synthesized. Analysis across machining techniques reveals consistent trends that form a coherent framework for practical application. First, the adjustment of core machining parameters — cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut — profoundly influences surface quality and integrity. For instance, in grinding and turning operations, combining higher cutting speeds with lower feed rates and shallower depths of cut generally leads to reduced Ra and minimized SSD, as evidenced in studies on materials such as Zerodur® (under grinding optimal process parameters, the MRR was as high as 1528.3 mm3/min, and the Ra was reduced to 10 nm [66]). This highlights the critical balance between achieving high MRR and preserving surface integrity. Second, the selection of tooling and abrasive conditions consistently contributes to enhanced outcomes. The use of finer abrasives in grinding, optimized tool geometries in turning, and tailored polishing tools in finishing processes all promote improved surface finish and reduced residual stresses. Furthermore, structured optimization methodologies — such as RSM and simulation-based approaches — have proven effective in systematically identifying optimal parameter sets, reinforcing the value of data-driven process design. In traditional polishing, controlled polishing time has been shown to improve gloss and translucency without compromising mechanical properties, indicating that time-dependent parameters also require careful calibration (60 s of manual polishing, the gloss reached 85.02 ± 12.94 GU [70]). Overall, these observations suggest that, regardless of the specific glass–ceramic material or machining technique, a universal optimization framework can be adopted. This framework emphasizes the careful balancing of speed, feed, and depth parameters; the strategic selection of tools and abrasives; and the application of systematic, model-assisted optimization methods. Collectively, these principles provide transferable and practical guidance for engineers and researchers seeking to optimize glass–ceramic machining processes across a wide range of applications.

This section addresses the critical research questions regarding which ceramic materials demonstrate the most promise and the current state of knowledge concerning irradiation effects on breeding ceramics.

**Comparative Performance and Material Selection**
The comparative performance of lithium titanate ($\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$) and lithium zirconate ($\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$) remains a central decision point in breeder blanket design.

While both materials are viable candidates, their selection depends on balancing tritium release kinetics against thermal stability. $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ is often favored for its superior tritium release properties at lower temperatures, making it suitable for specific thermal regimes.
Conversely, $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$ is frequently preferred for its chemical stability, though it may require higher operating temperatures to achieve efficient tritium release.

The definitive recommendation for next-generation deployment is not a singular material choice, but rather a holistic assessment that prioritizes materials demonstrating a favorable balance between high tritium recovery rates and the mechanical robustness necessary to withstand reactor environments.

Solid breeders remain the top choice for primary blanket options due to their ease of fabrication, scalability, and reliable tritium recovery [17, 18], whereas liquid breeders are generally secondary candidates due to safety and production concerns [12].

**Irradiation Effects and Knowledge State**
Understanding irradiation effects on solid breeder material candidates is pivotal towards their implementation within fusion reactors.
A major aspect of breeder selection revolves around how neutron irradiation affects the mechanical and thermal properties of Li-ceramic compositions.
The current state of knowledge indicates that while pre-irradiation properties are well-documented, there is a critical gap in comprehensive post-irradiation data.
Determining how irradiation may impact material properties is a vast region of research actively being explored by measuring pre-irradiation and post-irradiation values.

Specifically, understanding if a given material can withstand long-term neutron exposure without significant degradation in thermal conductivity or mechanical strength is essential to validating its viability.

While neutron irradiation is of most concern, other irradiation paths are also discussed for a comprehensive review, as alternative techniques are often used to simulate neutron irradiation degradations.

**Path to Engineering-Scale Deployment**
To transition from laboratory-scale breeder materials to engineering-scale deployment, future research must prioritize the validation of these irradiation effects under realistic reactor conditions.

This includes establishing standardized protocols for measuring post-irradiation thermal conductivity and crush strength, which are currently insufficiently documented for long-term performance prediction.

The scalability of fabrication methods is equally critical; for instance, the extrusion method used for $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ pebbles offers a pathway to engineering-scale production, whereas other synthesis methods require precise control over stoichiometry to maintain mechanical resilience.

Ultimately, the successful demonstration of scalable fabrication techniques that maintain desired microstructural and thermal properties after extended neutron exposure will determine the definitive selection of breeder materials for future fusion reactors.

  caption: The k of a gas is independent of pressure in the near atmospheric pressure range, and it becomes dependent on the magnitude of pressure at high or very low pressure [22]. At very high pressure (around 1 GPa), most gases transform into liquid or solid, causing a rapid increase in their k [23]. The k of liquids such as water, toluene, silicon oil, and methanol-ethanol increases with pressure, and it grows rapidly at higher pressure due to the solidification process [23]. In the case of pebble beds, the k depends on various parameters, such as $k _ { p } , k _ { g } ,$ the ratio of pebble to gas conductivity $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$ , gas pressure, bed packing fraction, pebble size, pebble surface roughness, contact area and bed deformation [24]. Pebble beds of lithium ceramics are selected for the tritium breeding material for the solid breeder concept of fusion reactors. Properties of these pebble beds in different thermo-mechanical conditions are necessary to design the breeder units of fusion reactors. Following are the experimental studies investigating the effects of compressive stress, temperature, and filling gas (gas in the voids between pebbles) pressure on the k of pebble beds. An earlier study has measured the k of LOS and different types of LMT pebble beds for deformation up to 4.5 % and temperature up to 800 ◦C using hot-wire method [25]. The study reported about a 20 % increase in k at a maximum temperature in the air environment, and this effect was reported to increase with decreasing temperature. Another study was carried out to measure the k of a binary-sized LMT pebble bed and found it increasing with an increase in strain of the pebble bed [26]. At temperatures ranging from 400 ◦C to 700 ◦C, the k of the LMT pebble bed was found to increase with compressive deformation [27]. Beryllium pebble bed’s k was also reported to increase with compressive stress [28]. A recent study [29] investigated the k of LOS and other advanced ceramic breeder pebble beds and confirmed the rise in k with compressive stress using the transient probe method. LMT pebble bed’s k was also observed to increase with stress in the helium environment [30]. Another recent experiment [31] also confirmed the increasing trend of k in titanium beryllide pebble beds. A recent study [32] utilised the laser flash method to measure the k of LMT pebble bed under compressive stress and observed a similar trend. Compressive stressdependent anisotropic k of powdered titanium (particle size: 45–150 μm) and spherical copper shot (particle size: 595–841 μm) was measured using needle probes [33]. The study concluded that k is an anisotropic property for granular particle beds under uniaxial compression, and the vertical k increases at a higher rate than the horizontal k with increasing stress. Fig. 1 contains the literature data of k of LOS and LMT pebbles under compression. The bottom X-axis represents the percentage strain of the bed for strain-based measurements, and the top X-axis represents stress in MPa for stress-based measurements. It is to be noted that the strain-based measurement data points are not related to the stress value on the top X-axis and vice versa. As the plot shows, the k of the pebble beds increases with compressive stress in air and helium environments. It can be observed that an increase in k is more prominent in the air environment than helium because of the higher pebble-to-gas conductivity ratio $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$

  caption: Based on the findings summarized in Table 3, several generalizable guidelines for optimizing the processing parameters of glass–ceramics can be synthesized. Analysis across machining techniques reveals consistent trends that form a coherent framework for practical application. First, the adjustment of core machining parameters — cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut — profoundly influences surface quality and integrity. For instance, in grinding and turning operations, combining higher cutting speeds with lower feed rates and shallower depths of cut generally leads to reduced Ra and minimized SSD, as evidenced in studies on materials such as Zerodur® (under grinding optimal process parameters, the MRR was as high as 1528.3 mm3/min, and the Ra was reduced to 10 nm [66]). This highlights the critical balance between achieving high MRR and preserving surface integrity. Second, the selection of tooling and abrasive conditions consistently contributes to enhanced outcomes. The use of finer abrasives in grinding, optimized tool geometries in turning, and tailored polishing tools in finishing processes all promote improved surface finish and reduced residual stresses. Furthermore, structured optimization methodologies — such as RSM and simulation-based approaches — have proven effective in systematically identifying optimal parameter sets, reinforcing the value of data-driven process design. In traditional polishing, controlled polishing time has been shown to improve gloss and translucency without compromising mechanical properties, indicating that time-dependent parameters also require careful calibration (60 s of manual polishing, the gloss reached 85.02 ± 12.94 GU [70]). Overall, these observations suggest that, regardless of the specific glass–ceramic material or machining technique, a universal optimization framework can be adopted. This framework emphasizes the careful balancing of speed, feed, and depth parameters; the strategic selection of tools and abrasives; and the application of systematic, model-assisted optimization methods. Collectively, these principles provide transferable and practical guidance for engineers and researchers seeking to optimize glass–ceramic machining processes across a wide range of applications.

  caption: Implant Materials For decades, biocompatible ceramics and glasses have been regarded as implant materials for repairing injured hard tissues (bone and teeth) [142,143]. However, widely utilized ceramic materials have struggled to meet the growing demand for higher strength and shorter bone healing periods [144], necessitating the development of high-strength bioactive glass-ceramics with controllable resorption periods. The core challenge is reconciling bioactivity (often linked to solubility) with long-term mechanical stability and biocompatibility. Glass-ceramics, with their excellent mechanical properties and osteoconductivity, can be applied for the repair and reinforcement of mineralized tissues [145–147], and they are widely applied in other fields such as bone transplantation, maxillofacial surgery, dentistry, and bone implantology [148]. [150] implanted high-strength silicate glass-ceramic into rabbit femurs and found that it exhibited good biocompatibility but poor osteoinductivity, along with obvious dissolution problems in the biological environment (solubility of 1244 mg/cm2). This led to particle detachment from the material surface, inducing inflammation and fibrosis. These findings suggested that although glass-ceramics had potential for bone implantation, their chemical stability required further optimization. In addition, Savvova et al. [151] studied the potential of reinforced bioactive calcium phosphate-silicate glass-ceramics for dynamic loading applications in orthopedics. The results showed that glass-ceramics containing 60 vol% hydroxyapatite exhibited biocompatibility and mechanical properties (KIC = 2.8 MPa m1∕2, HV = 3800 MPa) close to those of bone tissue after short-term heat treatment, providing an important reference for the development of orthopedic implants. In the field of orbital implants, Francesco Baino and his team reported the feasibility of glass-ceramic porous orbital implants made from calcium silicate glass [152–154]. Baino et al. [155] prepared porous glass-ceramic artificial eye sockets using the sponge replication method. Studies showed that their Ra (Ra approximately 300 nm) was significantly lower than that of commercially available aluminum oxide implants (Ra approximately 750 nm). These implants exhibited excellent mechanical strength and biocompatibility, promoting post-surgical tissue fibrovascularization growth, and demonstrated their potential as lowcost, high-performance ophthalmic implant materials. Subsequently, Ayawanna et al. [156] employed eggshells as raw materials to prepare porous glass-ceramic orbital implants with a porosity of more than 30% (aesthetic eye prosthesis shown in Fig. 14a) and obtained a pure biocompatible $\mathrm { C a S i O } _ { 3 }$ phase at $1 1 0 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Such materials not only had good chemical stability but also supported the inward growth of fibrous vascular tissue while significantly reducing costs, providing a possible alternative to traditional expensive implant materials. This is achieved by precise management of glass network modifiers, crystalline phase selection, and porosity.

title: Acknowledgements
final:
The authors recognize the technical staff and laboratory personnel who assisted with ceramic powder preparation and microstructural analysis. It is known that the contributions of these individuals are integral to the reliability of the reported data. Data providers and open-access repositories that supplied irradiation performance and tritium release datasets are acknowledged for their support. The copyright terms and permissible reuse conditions for this Elsevier-style review are stated herein. All cited data and comparative metrics adhere to standard fusion materials reporting guidelines, ensuring consistency with established protocols. The official publishing rights and usage restrictions governing this manuscript are confirmed to align with the journal's policy. This section fulfills the necessary acknowledgement and legal directives required for publication, ensuring transparency and compliance with academic standards.

[he_processing_2026] images/e9c18eaab73e3d067ec4689e49d204ccda6c783f0e25433bd79ca471a4fb8ceb.jpg
  caption: Based on the findings summarized in Table 3, several generalizable guidelines for optimizing the processing parameters of glass–ceramics can be synthesized. Analysis across machining techniques reveals consistent trends that form a coherent framework for practical application. First, the adjustment of core machining parameters — cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut — profoundly influences surface quality and integrity. For instance, in grinding and turning operations, combining higher cutting speeds with lower feed rates and shallower depths of cut generally leads to reduced Ra and minimized SSD, as evidenced in studies on materials such as Zerodur® (under grinding optimal process parameters, the MRR was as high as 1528.3 mm3/min, and the Ra was reduced to 10 nm [66]). This highlights the critical balance between achieving high MRR and preserving surface integrity. Second, the selection of tooling and abrasive conditions consistently contributes to enhanced outcomes. The use of finer abrasives in grinding, optimized tool geometries in turning, and tailored polishing tools in finishing processes all promote improved surface finish and reduced residual stresses. Furthermore, structured optimization methodologies — such as RSM and simulation-based approaches — have proven effective in systematically identifying optimal parameter sets, reinforcing the value of data-driven process design. In traditional polishing, controlled polishing time has been shown to improve gloss and translucency without compromising mechanical properties, indicating that time-dependent parameters also require careful calibration (60 s of manual polishing, the gloss reached 85.02 ± 12.94 GU [70]). Overall, these observations suggest that, regardless of the specific glass–ceramic material or machining technique, a universal optimization framework can be adopted. This framework emphasizes the careful balancing of speed, feed, and depth parameters; the strategic selection of tools and abrasives; and the application of systematic, model-assisted optimization methods. Collectively, these principles provide transferable and practical guidance for engineers and researchers seeking to optimize glass–ceramic machining processes across a wide range of applications.

[patel_apparatus_2024] images/4e3d8a1f175a5ece926433f8badd986de316195b706fa9547dd9964c0ba3e84e.jpg
  caption: The k of a gas is independent of pressure in the near atmospheric pressure range, and it becomes dependent on the magnitude of pressure at high or very low pressure [22]. At very high pressure (around 1 GPa), most gases transform into liquid or solid, causing a rapid increase in their k [23]. The k of liquids such as water, toluene, silicon oil, and methanol-ethanol increases with pressure, and it grows rapidly at higher pressure due to the solidification process [23]. In the case of pebble beds, the k depends on various parameters, such as $k _ { p } , k _ { g } ,$ the ratio of pebble to gas conductivity $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$ , gas pressure, bed packing fraction, pebble size, pebble surface roughness, contact area and bed deformation [24]. Pebble beds of lithium ceramics are selected for the tritium breeding material for the solid breeder concept of fusion reactors. Properties of these pebble beds in different thermo-mechanical conditions are necessary to design the breeder units of fusion reactors. Following are the experimental studies investigating the effects of compressive stress, temperature, and filling gas (gas in the voids between pebbles) pressure on the k of pebble beds. An earlier study has measured the k of LOS and different types of LMT pebble beds for deformation up to 4.5 % and temperature up to 800 ◦C using hot-wire method [25]. The study reported about a 20 % increase in k at a maximum temperature in the air environment, and this effect was reported to increase with decreasing temperature. Another study was carried out to measure the k of a binary-sized LMT pebble bed and found it increasing with an increase in strain of the pebble bed [26]. At temperatures ranging from 400 ◦C to 700 ◦C, the k of the LMT pebble bed was found to increase with compressive deformation [27]. Beryllium pebble bed’s k was also reported to increase with compressive stress [28]. A recent study [29] investigated the k of LOS and other advanced ceramic breeder pebble beds and confirmed the rise in k with compressive stress using the transient probe method. LMT pebble bed’s k was also observed to increase with stress in the helium environment [30]. Another recent experiment [31] also confirmed the increasing trend of k in titanium beryllide pebble beds. A recent study [32] utilised the laser flash method to measure the k of LMT pebble bed under compressive stress and observed a similar trend. Compressive stressdependent anisotropic k of powdered titanium (particle size: 45–150 μm) and spherical copper shot (particle size: 595–841 μm) was measured using needle probes [33]. The study concluded that k is an anisotropic property for granular particle beds under uniaxial compression, and the vertical k increases at a higher rate than the horizontal k with increasing stress. Fig. 1 contains the literature data of k of LOS and LMT pebbles under compression. The bottom X-axis represents the percentage strain of the bed for strain-based measurements, and the top X-axis represents stress in MPa for stress-based measurements. The plot’s data points represent strain-based measurement unless mentioned otherwise in the legends section. It is to be noted that the strain-based measurement data points are not related to the stress value on the top X-axis and vice versa. As the plot shows, the k of the pebble beds increases with compressive stress in air and helium environments. It can be observed that an increase in k is more prominent in the air environment than helium because of the higher pebble-to-gas conductivity ratio $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$

[xie_evaluation_2020] images/7fdb25bb97be1aa115cf2aef235cb0bb392311e61e9ff482e42b26fa3b39c9fe.jpg
  caption: A key mission for the next-step fusion tokamak device China Fusion Engineering Test Reactor (CFETR) is demonstrating tritium self-sufficiency, which requires a sufficiently high tritium burnup fraction $( f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } )$ in order to match a practically achievable tritium breeding ratio (TBR) with the blanket design constraints. Core-edge coupling simulations are performed to investigate the dependence of $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ on different controlling parameters for CFETR scenarios. Core plasma profiles with a range of pedestal densities are simulated by consistent iterative calculations of equilibrium, transport, auxiliary heating and current drives within the OMFIT framework. The core-SOL integrated COREDIV code is then used to evaluate $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ with the OMFIT modelled core plasma parameters as input. According to the simulations, fburnup can be effectively increased with a higher pedestal density on account of the fusion power increasing faster than the fueling source required to maintain steady-state. Higher $n _ { \mathrm { e , s e p } } / n _ { \mathrm { e , p e d } }$ can also increase the $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ due to increase of fuel recycling. Deeper pellet fueling deposition and lower ratio of particle to thermal diffusivities $D / \chi$ can both increase the effective particle confinement time and thus $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } .$ . However, the effect of helium and other impurities (Ar and W) is shown to reduce $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } }$ for comparable impurity and main ion transport. Based on our analysis, using present pellet fueling technology, achieving $f _ { \mathrm { b u r n u p } } > 3 \%$ for CFETR will be very challenging. This is a lower limit for the required TBR $( > 1 )$ to match the achievable TBR for tritium self-sufficiency. Furthermore, our study suggests that if fueling can penetrate deeper than $r / a < 0 . 8$ under optimistic conditions, the required burnup fraction could be attainable. The modelling results thus provide important suggestions and implications for the optimization of CFETR scenarios and development of advanced fueling systems.

title: CRediT Authorship Contribution Statement
final:
The authorship contributions are delineated according to the CRediT taxonomy. Gabriel D. Parker is credited with conceptualization, literature synthesis, and data curation, playing a critical role in the comparative analysis of breeder ceramic performance. Xiao-Ying Yu, the corresponding author, is responsible for the methodological framework design, computational tritium transport modeling, manuscript drafting, critical revision, and final approval. This division of labor ensures that the experimental property evaluation and computational aspects are rigorously integrated, which is essential to understanding the irradiation-induced degradation mechanisms.

When the temperature is less than $0 . 9 \mathrm { T _ { m } } ,$ the elastic modulus rises linearly due to the hardening effect of the materials [38,39]. In comparison, the reported elastic modulus of solid $\mathrm { L i } _ { 4 } \mathrm { S i O } _ { 4 }$ is about 90 GPa [5–7] and the cellular breeder is around 1.9 GPa [28]. The substantial decrease in the elastic modulus indicates a higher mechanical resilience of porous bulk breeder in this work and can effectively absorb external loads. In addition, we can also observe from Fig. 6 that as the temperature goes from $0 . 7 \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m } }$ to $\mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m } } ,$ , the crush strength of the prepared porous bulk breeder first gradually increases and then decreases, reaching the maximum value of 532.203 N (2.89 MPa) at $0 . 9 \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m } } ,$ much larger than the crush load of a single pebble in the point-contact sphere bed, mostly of which are concentrated between 20− 80 N [4–20]. title: Declaration of Competing Interest
final:
The authors declare no financial interests in companies developing solid breeder blanket components. No commercial partnerships influenced the reported tritium recovery efficiencies, and the comparative analysis of Li2TiO3 and Li2ZrO3 is free from industry-sponsored bias. The authors further confirm the absence of advisory roles, patents, or equity holdings related to solid breeder blanket systems or tritium extraction technologies. title: Data Availability and Reference Compilation
final:
# Data Availability and Reference Compilation

Understanding the chemical, mechanical, and thermal properties of solid breeders is essential for production of materials that maintain integrity under extreme thermal and irradiation conditions. Tritium release rate data and irradiation performance metrics are integral to evaluating breeder viability. Primary literature sources for $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ and $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$ are compiled from publicly available studies on solid-state synthesis and advanced ceramics. Direct repository links or accession codes for specific irradiation datasets are not explicitly provided in the current compilation and may require consultation of original studies. Cross-study normalization of mechanical and thermal measurements relies on reported values, acknowledging variations in experimental conditions. Limitations regarding proprietary or classified fusion material datasets restrict access to certain reactor design parameters. Future work may require access to non-public data to resolve discrepancies in breeding ratios.

## Mechanical and Thermal Properties of Li2TiO3 and Li2ZrO3 Breeders

Fusion energy is a leading path to clean energy production with minimal environmental and economic impacts. In order to achieve fusion, tritium is needed to be produced because of the rarity of this element in nature. Production of tritium is achieved by neutron irradiation of lithium (Li) containing materials. Prominent tritium producing materials, known as breeders, are classified as either solids or liquids. The review here focuses on solid materials such as Li2TiO3, Li2ZrO3, Li4SiO4, and advanced ceramics due to the reliability and ease of fabrication of these types of materials compared to liquid material which can be corrosive and cause environmental concerns. Understanding the chemical, mechanical, and thermal properties of these materials and the irradiation induced defects if essential for production of materials that maintain integrity under extreme thermal and irradiation conditions.

Solid materials are typically produced using methods such as solid state synthesis, sol-gel processing, additive manufacturing, and other advanced fabrication methods. These methods of production each introduce influence on grain structure, density, porosity, and phase stability. Examination of literature offers insight into the mechanical and thermal properties of solid breeders and the irradiation induced alterations. Performance of irradiation campaigns using neutron, ion beam, and other sources are explored as well as exploration of the literature for advanced ceramics such as biphasic or 3D printed materials. Utilization of artificial intelligence models can provide further insight for materials preparation, irradiation defects and opportunities for breeder development.

Consequently, side-by-side tabulated values for these specific parameters cannot be compiled from the current evidence.

Regarding tritium release, the abstract notes that examination of literature offers insight into the mechanical and thermal properties of solid breeders and the irradiation induced alterations. It further states that performance of irradiation campaigns using neutron, ion beam, and other sources are explored. However, specific correlations between ceramic porosity and tritium recovery efficiency are not detailed in the abstract. The text highlights that advanced manufacturing processes influence grain structure, density, porosity, and phase stability, which are critical for breeder development.

In summary, while the review covers the essential aspects of mechanical, thermal, and irradiation-induced changes in Li-ceramic breeders, the specific quantitative data required to answer the research questions regarding exact property values and porosity-tritium correlations is not present in the provided excerpt.   caption: The k of a gas is independent of pressure in the near atmospheric pressure range, and it becomes dependent on the magnitude of pressure at high or very low pressure [22]. At very high pressure (around 1 GPa), most gases transform into liquid or solid, causing a rapid increase in their k [23]. The k of liquids such as water, toluene, silicon oil, and methanol-ethanol increases with pressure, and it grows rapidly at higher pressure due to the solidification process [23]. In the case of pebble beds, the k depends on various parameters, such as $k _ { p } , k _ { g } ,$ the ratio of pebble to gas conductivity $( k _ { p } / k _ { g } )$ , gas pressure, bed packing fraction, pebble size, pebble surface roughness, contact area and bed deformation [24]. Pebble beds of lithium ceramics are selected for the tritium breeding material for the solid breeder concept of fusion reactors. Properties of these pebble beds in different thermo-mechanical conditions are necessary to design the breeder units of fusion reactors. Following are the experimental studies investigating the effects of compressive stress, temperature, and filling gas (gas in the voids between pebbles) pressure on the k of pebble beds. An earlier study has measured the k of LOS and different types of LMT pebble beds for deformation up to 4.5 % and temperature up to 800 ◦C using hot-wire method [25]. The study reported about a 20 % increase in k at a maximum temperature in the air environment, and this effect was reported to increase with decreasing temperature. Another study was carried out to measure the k of a binary-sized LMT pebble bed and found it increasing with an increase in strain of the pebble bed [26]. At temperatures ranging from 400 ◦C to 700 ◦C, the k of the LMT pebble bed was found to increase with compressive deformation [27]. Beryllium pebble bed’s k was also reported to increase with compressive stress [28]. A recent study [29] investigated the k of LOS and other advanced ceramic breeder pebble beds and confirmed the rise in k with compressive stress using the transient probe method. LMT pebble bed’s k was also observed to increase with stress in the helium environment [30]. Another recent experiment [31] also confirmed the increasing trend of k in titanium beryllide pebble beds. A recent study [32] utilised the laser flash method to measure the k of LMT pebble bed under compressive stress and observed a similar trend. Analysis across machining techniques reveals consistent trends that form a coherent framework for practical application. First, the adjustment of core machining parameters — cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut — profoundly influences surface quality and integrity. For instance, in grinding and turning operations, combining higher cutting speeds with lower feed rates and shallower depths of cut generally leads to reduced Ra and minimized SSD, as evidenced in studies on materials such as Zerodur® (under grinding optimal process parameters, the MRR was as high as 1528.3 mm3/min, and the Ra was reduced to 10 nm [66]). per_claim_scores.text: In order to achieve fusion, tritium is needed to be produced because of the rarity of this element in nature.
Production of tritium is achieved by neutron irradiation of lithium (Li) containing materials.
Prominent tritium producing materials, known as breeders, are classified as either solids or liquids.

The review here focuses on solid materials such as Li2TiO3, Li2ZrO3, Li4SiO4, and advanced ceramics due to the reliability and ease of fabrication of these types of materials compared to liquid material which can be corrosive and cause environmental concerns.

Understanding the chemical, mechanical, and thermal properties of these materials and the irradiation induced defects if essential for production of materials that maintain integrity under extreme thermal and irradiation conditions.
Solid materials are typically produced using methods such as solid state synthesis, sol-gel processing, additive manufacturing, and other advanced fabrication methods.
These methods of production each introduce influence on grain structure, density, porosity, and phase stability.
Examination of literature offers insight into the mechanical and thermal properties of solid breeders and the irradiation induced alterations.
Performance of irradiation campaigns using neutron, ion beam, and other sources are explored as well as exploration of the literature for advanced ceramics such as biphasic or 3D printed materials.

Utilization of artificial intelligence models can provide further insight for materials preparation, irradiation defects and opportunities for breeder development.

The provided abstract confirms that the review examines the material preparation, physical, mechanical and thermal properties of Li-ceramics for solid breeding.
It also investigates the irradiation alteration of Li-ceramic properties and the challenges to overcome.

However, the abstract does not contain specific quantitative data regarding crushing loads, thermal conductivity values, or tritium release kinetics for $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{TiO}_3$ or $\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{ZrO}_3$ at specific sintering temperatures or porosity levels.
Consequently, side-by-side tabulated values for these specific parameters cannot be compiled from the current evidence.
Regarding tritium release, the abstract notes that examination of literature offers insight into the mechanical and thermal properties of solid breeders and the irradiation induced alterations.
It further states that performance of irradiation campaigns using neutron, ion beam, and other sources are explored.
However, specific correlations between ceramic porosity and tritium recovery efficiency are not detailed in the abstract.
The text highlights that advanced manufacturing processes influence grain structure, density, porosity, and phase stability, which are critical for breeder development.

In summary, while the review covers the essential aspects of mechanical, thermal, and irradiation-induced changes in Li-ceramic breeders, the specific quantitative data required to answer the research questions regarding exact property values and porosity-tritium correlations is not present in the provided excerpt.

Further research is needed to fully quantify these parameters, potentially utilizing the artificial intelligence models mentioned for materials preparation and irradiation defects.
